entry.summary: I wanted a simpler way to launch a compatible ChatGPT installation with a local HTTP proxy while leaving my Mac’s system proxy and DNS settings alone. Switching system-wide settings was inconvenient when other applications needed different configurations. I built Local Route Launcher, a free, MIT-licensed utility written in SwiftUI and AppKit. entry.title: Stop asking AI to “clean this up”: a safe refactoring loop (with 2 free prompts)
entry.summary:
Ask Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT to “clean this up” or “refactor this,” and you’ll usually get something: new folders, renamed symbols, a fashionable pattern, maybe a dependency bump. Sometimes it’s even an improvement. Often it’s an unreviewable rewrite. The diff mixes structure with silent behaviour changes. Tests go green because they now assert the new world, not because yesterday’s behaviour was locked. Reviewers approve the vibe and miss the logic edit in the noise. AI isn’t bad at refactoring. “Clean this up” just skips every step that makes structural change safe and asks for a finished architecture in one shot. entry.title: How I Actually Prove an Offline App Is Offline (Not Just Trust the Marketing)
entry.summary: "Runs offline" is the easiest claim in software to make and one of the least frequently checked. I build an offline AI app, so I'm on the hook for the claim — here's the testing I actually run, which is the same thing you could run against anything else that claims it. 1. Disable the network adapter, not just Wi-Fi. 2. Watch the filesystem, not the app. 3. Search the whole machine after unplugging. 4. Check it in a state you didn't design for. What I got wrong first time: Why bother being this strict about it? If you've got a sharper method than the four above — particularly for catching network calls a process makes before you've started watching it — I'd like to hear it. The app, if you want to run these tests against it yourself: getpocketcore.com

entry.title: git bisect run named the wrong commit 10 out of 10 times — so I gave every commit its own clean room
entry.summary:
git bisect run is the right algorithm. What I did not expect is how confidently it lies when you leave it running unattended. I generated a 255-commit Python history in which a dependency pin (pytz) moves from 2022.1 to 2023.3 at commit 150, together with the golden value of the failing test. Each commit's test is right under its own pin and wrong under the other. A real bug is planted at commit 173. Then I ran git bisect run on it ten times, in one reused virtualenv:
How Named Right
env built at the known-good ref the pytz bump 0 / 5
env built at the failing ref a changelog edit 0 / 5
fresh venv at every step the planted commit 5 / 5
Ten of ten wrong, both flavours. The fixture is built to drift, so that is by construction — what it shows is the mechanism: bisect trusts one …
